blocks.source: Vol IV, Closed-Loop Evaluation, § Trial Budgets, Stopping Rules, and Comparisons
blocks.md: While a million software unit tests consume only processor cycles, each closed-loop trial of a physical robot consumes test-cell time, exhausts bearing and linkage fatigue life, burns thermal headroom in motor windings, and risks costly hardware damage. Statistical theory dictates how many trials a reliability claim demands, but on a physical machine the plant, not the compute budget, determines what each trial costs.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Zero-failure bound matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: At zero failures the Wald interval collapses, so a clean record is inverted exactly (failure bound about 3/n), which makes twenty clean runs consistent with a one-in-seven failure rate and makes every added nine cost about ten times the trials.

questions.q: The section **Trial Budgets, Stopping Rules, and Comparisons** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Replay, closed-loop simulation, shadow operation, and constrained physical testing sit on two axes (causal feedback, physical realism) and each trades one distortion for another, so they are not a fidelity ladder.
Early acceptance is valid only under a boundary declared in advance (Wald's SPRT), and comparing two checkpoints needs interleaved, randomized, blinded runs on one unit.
Task completion, proposer autonomy, and supervisory burden are separate channels, and an intervened run is an autonomy failure, never a success that was cut short (the censored trial fallacy).

At zero failures the Wald interval collapses, so a clean record is inverted exactly (failure bound about 3/n), which makes twenty clean runs consistent with a one-in-seven failure rate and makes every added nine cost about ten times the trials.
